- **Last fall, I was running a tiny recruiting startup. Then I read this article, which showed administrative and patient care expenditures over the last 15 years. I was stunned. --- Healthcare admin is an unbelievably expensive, complex process. It's a trillion dollar problem: wrangling faxes, handwritten notes, making phone calls, etc just to assist the basics - helping patients get care from physicians. When Kesava Kirupa Dinakaran told me about the opportunity at Luminai, I had to lean in. Luminai is working directly with Cleveland Clinic and other large health systems to solve the burden of healthcare administration. It's been a thrilling ride getting to actually tackle the biggest problem in healthcare, with its most important players, with an unbelievably talented team. If you've been sitting on sidelines wondering what company to join next, text me. Our careers page is here: https://lnkd.in/d79mW2ey The opportunity at Luminai is huge - we are hiring the best of the best, and we're moving really quickly. And Cleveland is nice in the spring. :)**

- **Hi folks, After leaving Benchling , I was excited to try my hand outside of healthcare / life sciences, building something to make hiring better. That company became Partly . Building Partly with Collin Buchan , my co-founder, and our team of fractional operators (including Eli Berkowitz, My Pham , Brandon Henry, Andrew Guo , Kathy Garcia , Julian Sul , and Stefan Young , among many others) was a true pleasure. We built an amazing product, and helped a bunch of folks find fractional and full-time roles. It was a privilege to play even a small part in so many talented careers. For those of you who took a chance on us and used our software, thank you! :) After two years, I’m delighted to say that we sold our company to Luminai . As part of the transition, Collin and I joined the Luminai team. Kesava Kirupa Dinakaran and I were already friends before we started talking about working together. But our shared ambition to reimagine healthcare is what truly convinced us to join. It’s only been a couple of months, but I could not be more excited about what we’re building, and the opportunity we’re going after. And, as usual, I didn’t really switch jobs. Now I’m spending EVEN MORE TIME hiring, this time for forward deployed engineers. If you’re interested, would love to chat. Stay tuned for more company updates! Excited to be the next LinkedInfluencer. Sanjay**

- **You can't go a week in tech these days without seeing another “ex-Palantir founder raises a bajillion dollars” headline. I am now, improbably, one of those founders (minus a few zillion), even though I never thought I’d start a company. But at some point in the last year, I began to think that *not* starting one was actually the riskier choice. I’ve spent a long time thinking about how that inversion happened. - **Many of you know I left Seqera back in December. In addition to doing advisory work, I also wrote a book! My dad spent 40 years as an amateur historian, researching our family history. He compiled 66,000 words of primary source research that nobody outside the family had ever seen. Our family came from Ireland during the famine, fought in the Civil War, and ended up in Tombstone, Arizona. My great-great-great grandfather Nicholas McCormick was murdered in 1887. After he died, the family's mining claims were sold for $350. They turned out to be worth millions. I took his research and turned it into a narrative nonfiction book. It's called Skin, Gristle & Bone: Forgotten Frontier Lives in the Shadow of Tombstone, and it's live on Amazon now. 200 pages built on forty years of research, written in about 30 days with Claude as a writing partner. That last part is its own story. I wrote a piece on Substack walking through everything I learned about using AI for long-form writing and self-publishing on Amazon, from the workflow decisions that actually mattered to what the AI got wrong and how I caught it. If you've ever thought about writing a book, it's worth a read. https://lnkd.in/g_HrKmF2 If the story sounds interesting, the Amazon link is below. And if you end up reading it, a review would mean a lot. https://lnkd.in/gmXQBGcv And before the ink was even dry, I started on my second book. It's the real story of what thirty years inside Silicon Valley startups looks like from up close. Stay tuned for updates.**

**Aditya Agarwal** (born 1982) is an Indian-American software engineer and investor. He is a general partner at the venture capital fund [South Park Commons](/wiki/South_Park_Commons "South Park Commons"). Agarwal was previously the [Chief Technology Officer](/wiki/Chief_Technology_Officer "Chief Technology Officer") (CTO) of [Dropbox](/wiki/Dropbox "Dropbox") and an early engineer at [Facebook](/wiki/Facebook "Facebook"), where he served as the first Director of Product Engineering.

## Education

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Aditya_Agarwal&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Education")]

Agarwal attended [Carnegie Mellon University](/wiki/Carnegie_Mellon_University "Carnegie Mellon University") (CMU) in [Pittsburgh, Pennsylvania](/wiki/Pittsburgh,_Pennsylvania "Pittsburgh, Pennsylvania"), where he earned both a Bachelor's and Master's degree in [Computer Science](/wiki/Computer_Science "Computer Science").[[1]](#cite_note-CMU_Profile-1)

## Career

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Aditya_Agarwal&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Career")]

### Facebook

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Aditya_Agarwal&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Facebook")]

Agarwal joined [Facebook](/wiki/Facebook "Facebook") as a software engineer in 2005.[[2]](#cite_note-EconomicTimes-2) He was one of the company's first engineers and helped build the initial search engine for the platform.[[3]](#cite_note-HindustanTimes-3) He eventually became the company's first Director of Product Engineering, where he oversaw engineering for products including Search.[[4]](#cite_note-4)

### Cove and Dropbox

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Aditya_Agarwal&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Cove and Dropbox")]

Agarwal co-founded Cove, a collaboration software company, with [Ruchi Sanghvi](/wiki/Ruchi_Sanghvi "Ruchi Sanghvi").[[5]](#cite_note-TechCrunch_Cove-5) In February 2012, [Dropbox](/wiki/Dropbox "Dropbox") acquired Cove, and Agarwal joined Dropbox as Vice President of Engineering.[[5]](#cite_note-TechCrunch_Cove-5)

In October 2016, Agarwal was appointed Chief Technology Officer (CTO) of Dropbox, succeeding co-founder [Arash Ferdowsi](/wiki/Arash_Ferdowsi "Arash Ferdowsi").[[6]](#cite_note-BusinessInsider_CTO-6) As CTO, he was responsible for the company's engineering, product, and technical operations. He left Dropbox in 2017.[[7]](#cite_note-TechCrunch_Leave-7)

### Investing

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Aditya_Agarwal&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: Investing")]

Agarwal is a partner at [South Park Commons](/wiki/South_Park_Commons "South Park Commons"), a venture capital fund and technologist community founded by Ruchi Sanghvi.[[8]](#cite_note-NYT_SPC-8)[[9]](#cite_note-SPC_Bio-9)

He has served on the board of directors of [Flipkart](/wiki/Flipkart "Flipkart"), an Indian e-commerce company, joining as an independent director in 2014.[[10]](#cite_note-Flipkart-10)

## Philanthropy and affiliations

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Aditya_Agarwal&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: Philanthropy and affiliations")]

In 2013, Agarwal was a founding contributor to [FWD.us](/wiki/FWD.us "FWD.us"), a 501(c)(4) lobbying group focused on immigration reform and education in the United States.[[11]](#cite_note-SFGate_FWD-11)

He has served on the board of trustees for the [Anita Borg Institute for Women and Technology](/wiki/Anita_Borg_Institute_for_Women_and_Technology "Anita Borg Institute for Women and Technology")[[12]](#cite_note-AnitaBorg-12) and on the advisory board for the School of Computer Science at Carnegie Mellon University.[[13]](#cite_note-CMU_Board-13)

Agarwal is a co-author of *The Holloway Guide to Technical Recruiting and Hiring* (2020), a reference book on engineering recruitment.[[14]](#cite_note-14)

## Personal life

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Aditya_Agarwal&action=edit&section=7 "Edit section: Personal life")]

Agarwal is married to [Ruchi Sanghvi](/wiki/Ruchi_Sanghvi "Ruchi Sanghvi"), a computer engineer and founder of [South Park Commons](/wiki/South_Park_Commons "South Park Commons"). They met while studying at [Carnegie Mellon University](/wiki/Carnegie_Mellon_University "Carnegie Mellon University") and later worked together at Facebook and Dropbox.[[1]](#cite_note-CMU_Profile-1) They married in 2010.[[2]](#cite_note-EconomicTimes-2)

[Aditya Agarwal](http://skymanaditya1.github.io)

![Aditya Agarwal](images/profile/adi_ny_crop.png)

I am a third-year EECS PhD student at MIT advised by professors [Leslie Kaelbling](https://people.csail.mit.edu/lpk/) and [Tomás Lozano-Pérez](https://people.csail.mit.edu/tlp/). I am part of the [Learning and Intelligent Systems (LIS)](https://lis.csail.mit.edu/) Group, and part of the broader [CSAIL](https://www.csail.mit.edu/) [Embodied Intelligence (EI)](https://ei.csail.mit.edu/) Group. I am broadly interested in task-aware perception and compositional reasoning for embodied agents, enabling robots to achieve open-ended tasks in dynamic environments.

Previously, I was a robotics perception intern at [Autodesk](https://www.research.autodesk.com/research-areas/science/robotics/), where I worked on fast and adaptable robotic perception and foundation models for multi-part automated robot assembly. I was also a visiting researcher at [REAL](https://montrealrobotics.ca/) at [Université de Montréal](https://www.umontreal.ca/en/) associated with [Mila](https://mila.quebec/en/) advised by Prof. [Liam Paull](https://liampaull.ca/), an intern at [Microsoft Research India](https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/research/lab/microsoft-research-india/), working on problems in the areas of Education, Skilling, and Healthcare, and a [MITACS](https://www.mitacs.ca/our-programs/globalink-research-internship-students/) research intern at the [University of Calgary](https://www.ucalgary.ca/), where I worked on characterizing and localizing an audio noise nuisance called the Ranchlands Hum, advised by [Prof. Mike Smith](https://contacts.ucalgary.ca/info/enel/profiles/168-42833).

I completed my Masters by research from [IIIT Hyderabad](https://www.iiit.ac.in/) in Computer Science and Engineering, advised by professors [C V Jawahar](https://scholar.google.com/citations?user=U9dH-DoAAAAJ&hl=en) and [Vinay Namboodiri](https://vinaypn.github.io/) in the computer vision ([CVIT](https://cvit.iiit.ac.in/)) lab and by professors [Madhava Krishna](https://scholar.google.co.in/citations?user=QDuPGHwAAAAJ&hl=en) and [Srinath Sridhar](https://cs.brown.edu/people/ssrinath/) (Brown University) in the robotics ([RRC](https://robotics.iiit.ac.in/)) lab. I completed my Bachelors from [PES University](https://pes.edu/) (formerly PESIT) Bangalore in Computer Science and Engineering.

**Research Interests:** My research focuses on developing algorithms that enable embodied agents to dynamically perceive and reason about the world in order to achieve open-ended tasks. Specifically, I study task-aware perception and compositional reasoning, enabling robots to dynamically construct task-relevant representations by combining multimodal perception with planning and policy learning methods. I also study novel and efficient ways of integrating representation learning with robot policy learning to improve generalization (across pose and viewpoint variations), sample efficiency (requiring fewer demonstrations), and data-collection efficiency (learning from human demonstrations and leveraging world models as a proxy for data generation).

Our approach enables robots to reason about occluded and unseen parts of objects and scenes, enhancing their ability to plan and execute manipulation tasks in complex, real-world settings. |

We demonstrate how the actuated neck supports better spatial awareness in training autonomous policies through imitation learning, reducing distribution shift compared to static wide-angle cameras. |

Tenenbaum](https://web.mit.edu/cocosci/josh.html), [Antonio Torralba](https://groups.csail.mit.edu/vision/torralbalab/), [Florian Shkurti](https://www.cs.toronto.edu/~florian/), [Liam Paull](https://liampaull.ca/)  [ICRA 2024](images/projects/concept_graphs_arxiv2023/2024_icra_concept_graphs.pdf)  [Paper /](images/projects/concept_graphs_arxiv2023/2024_icra_concept_graphs.pdf)  [Project Page /](https://concept-graphs.github.io/)  [Code /](https://github.com/concept-graphs/concept-graphs)  [Video](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=mRhNkQwRYnc)  We propose ConceptGraphs, an open-vocabulary graph-structured representations for 3D scenes, built by leveraging 2D foundation models and fusing their output to 3D by multiview association. The utility of this representation is demonstrated through downstream robotic planning tasks. |

|  | EDMP: Ensemble-of-costs-guided Diffusion for Motion Planning [Kallol Saha](https://kallol-saha.github.io/)\*, [Vishal Mandadi](https://vishal-2000.github.io/)\*, [Jayaram Reddy](https://scholar.google.com/citations?user=7XG2UgQAAAAJ&hl=en)\*, [Ajit Srikanth](https://scholar.google.com/citations?user=2yO8kZoAAAAJ&hl=en),  [Aditya Agarwal](https://skymanaditya1.github.io/) , [Bipasha Sen](https://bipashasen.github.io/), [Arun Singh](https://www.etis.ee/CV/Arun%20Kumar_Singh/eng/), [Madhava Krishna](https://www.iiit.ac.in/faculty/k-madhava-krishna/)  [ICRA 2024](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2309.11414.pdf)  [Paper /](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2309.11414.pdf)  [Project Page /](https://ensemble-of-costs-diffusion.github.io/)  [Code /](https://github.com/vishal-2000/EDMP)  [Video](https://youtu.be/F2UI0UNsdjo)  We propose EDMP for motion planning, that combines the strengths of classical motion planning (offering remarkable adaptability) and deep-learning-based motion planning (prior understanding over diverse valid trajectories). Our diffusion-based network is trained on a set of diverse kinematically valid trajectories. For any new scene at the time of inference, we compute scene-specific costs such as "collision cost" and guide the generation of valid trajectories that satisfy scene-specific constraints. |
|  | HyP-NeRF: Learning Improved NeRF Priors using a HyperNetwork [Bipasha Sen](https://bipashasen.github.io/)\*, [Gaurav Singh](https://vanhalen42.github.io/)\*,  [Aditya Agarwal](https://skymanaditya1.github.io/)\*  , [Madhava Krishna](https://www.iiit.ac.in/faculty/k-madhava-krishna/), [Srinath Sridhar](https://srinathsridhar.com/)  [NeurIPS 2023](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2306.06093.pdf)  [Paper /](images/projects/hypnerf_arxiv2023/HyP-NeRF.pdf)  [Code /](https://github.com/hyp-nerf/HyP-NeRF)  [Video](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=40JOIWJAvGs)  We propose HyP-NeRF, a latent conditioning method for learning generalizable category-level NeRF priors using hypernetworks. We use hypernetworks to estimate both the weights and the multi-resolution hash encodings resulting in significant quality gains. To further improve quality, we incorporate a denoise and finetune strategy that denoises images rendered from NeRFs estimated by the hypernetwork and finetunes it while retaining multiview consistency. |
|  | Disentangling Planning and Control for Non-prehensile Tabletop Manipulation [Vishal Reddy Mandadi](https://vishal-2000.github.io/), [Kallol Saha](https://kallol-saha.github.io/), [Dipanwita Guhathakurta](https://www.linkedin.com/in/dipanwita-guhathakurta/), [M. Nomaan Qureshi](https://qureshinomaan.github.io/),  [Aditya Agarwal](https://skymanaditya1.github.io/)  , [Bipasha Sen](https://bipashasen.github.io/), [Dipanjan Das](https://scholar.google.com/citations?user=HRZMDDsAAAAJ&hl=en), [Brojeshwar Bhowmick](https://sites.google.com/view/brojeshwar/home), [Arun Singh](https://www.etis.ee/CV/Arun%20Kumar_Singh/eng/), [Madhava Krishna](https://www.iiit.ac.in/faculty/k-madhava-krishna/)  [CASE 2023](https://case2023.org/)  [Paper](https://ieeexplore.ieee.org/stamp/stamp.jsp?tp=&arnumber=10260462)  We propose a framework that disentangles planning and control for tabletop manipulation in unknown scenes using a pushing-by-striking method (without tactile feedback) by explicitly modeling the object dynamics. Our method consists of two components: an A\* planner for path-planning and a low-level RL controller that models object dynamics. |
|  | SCARP: 3D Shape Completion in ARbitrary Poses for Improved Grasping [Bipasha Sen](https://bipashasen.github.io/)\*,  [Aditya Agarwal](https://skymanaditya1.github.io/)\*  , [Gaurav Singh](https://vanhalen42.github.io/)\*, [Brojeshwar Bhowmick](https://sites.google.com/view/brojeshwar/home), [Srinath Sridhar](https://srinathsridhar.com/), [Madhava Krishna](https://www.iiit.ac.in/faculty/k-madhava-krishna/)  [ICRA 2023](https://www.icra2023.org/)  [Paper /](images/projects/scarp_icra2023/ICRA_2429_published.pdf)  [Project Page /](https://bipashasen.github.io/scarp/)  [Short Video /](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=o2PuRVZ3jJA)  [Code /](https://github.com/vanhalen42/SCARP)  [Poster /](images/projects/scarp_icra2023/poster.pdf)  [Long Video](https://youtu.be/lyEc991wyTI)  We propose a mechanism for completing partial 3D shapes in arbitrary poses by learning a disentangled feature representation of pose and shape. We rely on learning rotationally equivariant pose features and geometric shape features by training a multi-tasking objective. SCARP improves the shape completion performance by 45% and grasp proposals by 71.2% over existing baselines. |
|  | FaceOff: A Video-to-Video Face Swapping System [Aditya Agarwal](https://skymanaditya1.github.io/)\*  , [Bipasha Sen](https://bipashasen.github.io/)\*, [Rudrabha Mukhopadhyay](https://rudrabha.github.io/), [Vinay P. Namboodiri](https://vinaypn.github.io/), [C.V. Jawahar](https://faculty.iiit.ac.in/~jawahar/)  [WACV 2023](https://wacv2023.thecvf.com/home)  [Paper /](https://openaccess.thecvf.com/content/WACV2023/papers/Agarwal_FaceOff_A_Video-to-Video_Face_Swapping_System_WACV_2023_paper.pdf)  [Project Page /](http://cvit.iiit.ac.in/research/projects/cvit-projects/faceoff)  [Video /](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=aNhs-mqMOcE)  [Poster /](images/projects/faceoff_wacv2023/615-wacv-post.pdf)  [Code /](https://github.com/skymanaditya1/FaceOff)  [Supplementary](images/projects/faceoff_wacv2023/0615-supp.pdf)  We propose a novel direction of video-to-video (V2V) face-swapping that tackles a pressing challenge in the moviemaking industry: swapping the actor's face and expressions on the face of their body double. Existing face-swapping methods preserve only the identity of the source face without swapping the expressions. In FaceOff, we swap the source's facial expressions along with the identity on the target's background and pose. |
|  | Towards MOOCs for Lipreading: Using Synthetic Talking Heads to Train Humans in Lipreading at Scale [Aditya Agarwal](https://skymanaditya1.github.io/)\*  , [Bipasha Sen](https://bipashasen.github.io/)\*, [Rudrabha Mukhopadhyay](https://rudrabha.github.io/), [Vinay P. Namboodiri](https://vinaypn.github.io/), [C.V. Jawahar](https://faculty.iiit.ac.in/~jawahar/)  [WACV 2023](https://wacv2023.thecvf.com/home)  [Paper /](https://openaccess.thecvf.com/content/WACV2023/papers/Agarwal_Towards_MOOCs_for_Lipreading_Using_Synthetic_Talking_Heads_To_Train_WACV_2023_paper.pdf)  [Project Page /](http://cvit.iiit.ac.in/research/projects/cvit-projects/mooc-lip)  [Video /](https://youtu.be/tc2Pt6dyjjo)  [Poster /](images/projects/moocs-lrt_wacv2023/720-wacv-post.pdf)  [Supplementary](images/projects/moocs-lrt_wacv2023/0720-supp.pdf)  Hard-of-hearing people rely on lipreading the mouth movements of the speaker to understand the spoken content. In this work, we developed computer vision techniques and built upon existing AI models, such as TTS and talking-face generation, to generate synthetic lipreading training content in any language. |
|  | INR-V: A Continuous Representation Space for Video-based Generative Tasks [Bipasha Sen](https://bipashasen.github.io/)\*,  [Aditya Agarwal](https://skymanaditya1.github.io/)\*  , [Vinay P. Namboodiri](https://vinaypn.github.io/), [C.V. Jawahar](https://faculty.iiit.ac.in/~jawahar/)  [TMLR 2022](https://www.jmlr.org/tmlr/)  [Paper /](https://openreview.net/pdf?id=aIoEkwc2oB)  [OpenReview /](https://openreview.net/forum?id=aIoEkwc2oB)  [Project Page /](/INRV/)  [Video /](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ViIwnu5vcck)  [Code](https://github.com/bipashasen/INRV)  Inspired by the recent works on parameterizing 3D shapes and scenes as Implicit Neural Representations (INRs), we encode videos as INRs. We train a hypernetwork to learn a prior over these INR functions and propose two techniques, i) Progressive Training and ii) Video-CLIP Regularization to stabilize hypernetwork training. INR-V shows remarkable performance on several video-generative tasks on many benchmark datasets. |
|  | Approaches and Challenges in Robotic Perception for Table-top Rearrangement and Planning [Aditya Agarwal](https://skymanaditya1.github.io/)\*  , [Bipasha Sen](https://bipashasen.github.io/)\*, [Shankara Narayanan V](https://marleyshan21.github.io/)\*, [Vishal Reddy Mandadi](https://vishal-2000.github.io/)\*, [Brojeshwar Bhowmick](https://sites.google.com/view/brojeshwar/home), [K Madhava Krishna](https://www.iiit.ac.in/faculty/k-madhava-krishna/)  [3rd in ICRA 2022 Open Cloud Table Organization Challenge](https://rpal.cse.usf.edu/rgmc_icra2022/)  [Paper /](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2205.04090.pdf)  [Competition /](https://rpal.cse.usf.edu/rgmc_icra2022/)  [Video /](https://youtu.be/5VSP49OB0ZI)  [Slides /](images/projects/ocrtoc_icra2022/WeeklyPresentations.pdf)  [Code /](https://github.com/skymanaditya1/ocrtoc_iiith/tree/jan30_sub_6dof)  [News1 /](https://blogs.iiit.ac.in/rrc/)  [News2](https://www.iiit.ac.in/files/media/Sakshi-RRC.jpeg)  In this challenge, we proposed an end-to-end pipeline in ROS incorporating the perception and planning stacks to manipulate objects from their initial configuration to a desired target configuration on a tabletop scene using a two-finger manipulator. The pipeline involves the following steps - (1) 3D scene registration, (2) Object pose estimation, (3) Grasp generation, (4) Task Planning, and (5) Motion Planning. |
|  | Personalized One-Shot Lipreading for an ALS Patient [Bipasha Sen](https://bipashasen.github.io/)\*,  [Aditya Agarwal](https://skymanaditya1.github.io/)\*  , [Rudrabha Mukhopadhyay](https://rudrabha.github.io/), [Vinay P. Namboodiri](https://vinaypn.github.io/), [C.V. Jawahar](https://faculty.iiit.ac.in/~jawahar/)  [BMVC 2021](https://www.bmvc2021-virtualconference.com/)  [Paper /](https://www.bmvc2021-virtualconference.com/assets/papers/1468.pdf)  [Video](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=_famGVaem-8)  We tackled the challenge of lipreading medical patients in a one-shot setting. There were two primary issues in training existing lipreading models - i) lipreading datasets had people suffering from no disabilities, ii) lipreading datasets lacked medical words. We devised a variational encoder-based domain adaptation technique to adapt models trained on large amounts of synthetic data to enable lipreading with one-shot real examples. |
|  | REED: An Approach Towards Quickly Bootstrapping Multilingual Acoustic Models [Bipasha Sen](https://bipashasen.github.io/)\*,  [Aditya Agarwal](https://skymanaditya1.github.io/)\*  , [Mirishkar Sai Ganesh](https://scholar.google.com/citations?user=URnA9a0AAAAJ&hl=en), [Anil Kumar Vuppala](https://www.iiit.ac.in/faculty/anil-kumar-vuppala/)  [SLT 2021](http://2021.ieeeslt.org/)  [Paper /](images/projects/reed_slt2021/reed_paper.pdf)  [Slides /](images/projects/reed_slt2021/reed_presentation.pdf)  [MLADS Paper](images/projects/reed_slt2021/MASR_Synapse.pdf)  We tackled the problem of building a multilingual acoustic model in a low-resource setting. We proposed a mechanism to bootstrap and validate the compatibility of multiple languages using CNNs operating directly on raw speech signals. Our method improves training and inference times by 4X and 7.4X, respectively, with comparable WERs against RNN-based baseline systems. |

# Aditya Agarwal

General Partner

Aditya Agarwal is a General Partner based in San Francisco. He was the CTO and VP of Engineering at Dropbox where he scaled the engineering team from 25 to 1000. Before Dropbox, Aditya co-founded Cove—a company that was building modern collaboration software. Prior to Cove, Aditya was one of Facebook’s first engineers. He helped build the first versions of key products like Search, NewsFeed and Messenger. He then became Facebook’s first director of Product Engineering, overseeing engineering for products like NewsFeed, Profile, Groups and Events. Aditya served on the boards of FlipKart—India’s leading e-commerce company, Carnegie Mellon’s School of Computer Science, and the Anita Borg Institute. He is also an active investor and advisor to Silicon Valley startups. In his spare time, Aditya likes to listen to techno music, read, travel and most of all, hang out with his two children. Aditya holds a bachelor's and master's degree in Computer Science from Carnegie Mellon University.

Aditya Agarwal, 34, is the chief technology officer of online file storage company Dropbox. He leads hundreds of software engineers in building tools used by Dropbox’s half a billion registered users. With a multibillion-dollar valuation, the privately held company is considered a heavyweight in the personal and business data storage industries.

---

### Computer kid

Born in India to a father who was a chemical engineer and mother who was a homemaker, Agarwal moved homes a lot with his family, with stints in Cameroon, Singapore, Malaysia, Indonesia and Thailand, before later settling in the United States. One of the constants in his life, though, was his love for computers.

“My dad got us a computer when I was 11 or 12 years old and I was always fascinated by the ability to program stuff,” he said. “I mean, it’s kind of a crazy thing, right? You’re sitting in your office or bedroom and you can build stuff that can do stuff. There’s something really intoxicating and powerful about that.”

Agarwal used books to teach himself to code, and later took programming classes in Indonesia. When it came time for college, he ventured to Carnegie Mellon University in Pittsburgh to study computer science.

### Creativity at Carnegie Mellon

One of the misconceptions about software engineering, Agarwal said, is that people tend to think of it as a mechanical job. He prefers to think of coding as a creative job.

“Writing a beautiful computer program is like building a work of art,” he said. “The best engineers are the ones who are able to reduce a problem to its simplest possible artifact. The ones who are not as good end up with these complicated solutions that are way more clunky.”

While studying his undergraduate and master’s degrees at Carnegie Mellon, Agarwal learned the programming languages of the day such as Java and C++. But more importantly, he learned the fundamentals of software engineering and the importance of thinking creatively. Referencing an analogy that Elon Musk once made, Agarwal likened his knowledge of computer science to a tree trunk and big branches, whose solid foundation allowed him to get to any leaf — or programming language — he wanted.

### Moving too slow

After graduation, many of Agarwal’s computer science peers were drawn to Wall Street because of the promise of making big bucks in the information technology departments of financial services corporations. Agarwal admits that he was close to pursuing a similar path, but said he could never convince himself that he cared enough about the kind of work he’d be expected to do.

“It’s nice to be rewarded and recognized, but you have to have intrinsic motivation around what you’re doing,” he said. “For me, that intrinsic motivation has always been that I need to be working at a place that is building products that I’m proud of.”

So while his classmates moved farther east to New York City, he went as far west as he could go, landing a job at Oracle in Silicon Valley.

“I’d been writing code for a year and I remember walking into my manager’s office and asking when we were going to get feedback from real users,” Agarwal said of his brief time at Oracle. “She looked at me and said, ‘Probably another three years.’ I was like, what do you mean? This is ridiculous. How will we know if we’re building the right thing?”

In that moment, he discovered he had another workplace deal breaker: He needed to be somewhere with a fast pace.

> If they can do it, why should I hold myself to a different standard? If they can learn, why can’t I learn?
>
> — Aditya Agarwal, chief technology officer of Dropbox

### Facebook

In the summer of 2005, Agarwal was introduced to Mark Zuckerberg, then the fresh-faced chief executive of a start-up called Facebook. Agarwal wasn’t a Facebook user, but walking into the company’s makeshift office in Palo Alto, he was buoyed by its energy.

“I thought, ‘Wow, this is about as polar opposite as you can get from the Oracle office,’” he said. “They were all wearing pajamas, there was cereal everywhere, there were still kegs there, a bunch of them were playing video games. But my God, the energy was great.”

On the advice of his then girlfriend (now wife), Agarwal joined the company as a software engineer. Facebook at the time had fewer than 15 employees. Agarwal was 22 years old.

“I was brought on to do whatever they asked me to do,” Agarwal said. “On my second day, Mark [Zuckerberg] said to me, ‘Hey, I need you to write Facebook’s search engine.’ I had no clue how to do that. I’d never built a search engine before. And I remember Mark looking at me and saying, ‘Yeah, I didn’t know how to write Facebook. So if I can write Facebook, why can’t you write the search engine?’ And yeah, that was logically consistent.”

### Learning to own it

Agarwal often had doubts about whether he was ready for the responsibilities given to him. At 24 he started managing Facebook’s engineers. He rose to be its first engineering director. By the time he left in 2010 to start his own company, Cove (which Dropbox acquired in 2012), he managed Facebook’s entire product engineering division. But he eased his doubts by drawing inspiration from the executives with whom he worked — first Zuckerberg at Facebook and later Drew Houston, chief executive of Dropbox.

“Mark and Drew had never been CEOs before, but they’re doing a fantastic job of it,” Agarwal said. “If they can do it, why should I hold myself to a different standard? If they can learn, why can’t I learn?”

He also found comfort in the idea that even though he wasn’t the best manager in the world because of his lack of experience, it was possible that he was the best manager for Facebook at that point because of his unique understanding of its products, people, culture and history.

“It was about having self-confidence and the ability to both be humble about the stuff I didn’t know, but also being confident about the stuff I did know,” he said.

### It’s all about the craft

As chief technology officer of Dropbox, Agarwal now spends his days recruiting, strategizing and delegating tasks instead of writing code. But he believes that anyone wanting to be a leader of a particular function within a company should have a deep understanding and appreciation for the craft they’re leading.

One of the things that he believes leaders at some of the most innovative companies in the world have in common — even if they don’t practice their craft every day — is “this super-honed intuition about what world-class looks like in their particular function,” Agarwal said. “If somebody’s trying to do what I do, my [advice] would be to become really good at the craft that you want to lead. Do not disassociate the actual craft from the act of leadership.”

For his part, he still codes for fun in his spare time, reads up on the latest programming languages and studies new technologies.

### Home with the family

Agarwal lives in San Francisco with his wife, Ruchi Sanghvi, who herself is a software engineer, entrepreneur and investor, and their 7-month-old son. He’s an avid reader of science fiction books and is a fan of cricket, soccer and tennis.

love building companies that, you know, the fact that I get to do that at my day job is something

spent a little bit of time in China as well. And then I came to America to go to university. I went to Carnegie Mellon for computer science, got a couple
of degrees, and then, unlike most of my friends who went to Wall Street to work for hedge funds, quant funds,
PE firms, consulting, I was like, I want to build software. So I moved out to the Bay Area and I worked at Oracle
for about a year, and Oracle had really interesting technical problems, but I was looking for something
that was more fast paced, that was kind of really kind of, you know, able to move a lot faster. I happened to get introduced
to Mark through a common friend. Mark was about 19 years old at that time.
He had just moved out from Harvard. You know, one, this is one
of the beautiful things of Silicon Valley. In Silicon Valley, people want to connect people. I had no idea who Mark was, and I'll be honest,
I had no idea what Facebook was because Facebook launched at Carnegie Mellon after I graduated. I had never used the product, so I went
to meet Mark because somebody said, this is a really, you know, passionate, intense young person. Go meet him.
See, you know, just you might enjoy the conversation. It was a short conversation with him.
It only lasted 15, 20 minutes. We discussed some of the technical challenges
and we discussed a little bit about like, hey, like why, why are you doing this? Why is this fun? I did not know much about the product, but I was
very sure that, like, I would have fun, like when I was working at Facebook and I would learn
from the people because they were also, like intense. They were driven, they were ambitious. I think that when people make decisions
about companies to start, I think oftentimes, you know, outside of Silicon Valley,
the question is like, oh, what did you see in the idea? Did you understand it was going to be such a big thing? And I think what they miss out is that early days,
you don't know, you can have a good idea. An idea that felt good could be bad, vice versa. But what you do know is that, like,
this is a person that I want to like, work with. Like, this is an interesting person who has interesting
ideas and we will iterate our way to build something great. And that's exactly how I felt about Mark.
I still remember when I decided to join Facebook. I called my mom and dad and they were like, you're crazy,
why are you leaving your well-paid, safe kind of job? You just got there. Why not spend like the next 3
or 4 years building up a base of savings? But I think I always was just like, man,
if I if I'm not going to take a risk when I'm 23, when am I going to take a risk? And then I spent the next six years and remember,
this was maybe about 3 or 4 months into joining Mark in the Facebook team. That Mark came up to me and he was just like, yo,
dude, you have to write a search engine for Facebook. And then my first thought was like,

yeah, we could or you could just write it. And guess what?

that why do you think you cannot do this is something that I hold very dearly. I strongly believe that if there's anything
that needs to be built given like time and energy, smart people can figure out things that they
otherwise don't know how to do, right? Otherwise, like, there's no way a startup has a right
to succeed because every founder eventually ends up having to do finance, marketing, sales. Right? They're not finance experts. They're not marketing experts,
they're not sales experts, but they figure it out. So I think that one episode has had a very big,
I would say, effect on my life in terms of how I think about what I'm able to do and I should be able to do. I am helping to guide the work of hundreds of engineers.
I've never managed hundreds of engineers. Why am I qualified for this job?
I would ask myself that question. Sure, there are plenty of people who might have managed
bigger, like who might be managing thousands of engineers. That doesn't mean that they're the right fit
to manage product engineering at Facebook, because I'm able to bring a certain amount of love
for the product context around the product. Historical legacy. In some ways, like I am intimately familiar with
everything that's kind of going on in this organization. So I think a lot of the times people tend to discount
their own experience and they think that like, oh, what I've done is not that interesting, but somebody
else has done something that's much more interesting. And I tell people like,
why don't discount your own experience? It actually might be much more relevant
to essentially what you're doing. I'd been at Facebook for 6 or 7 years,
and it was really one of the most remarkable moments in my life, if you will, because I just learned a lot. My time there was coming to an end. I decided that my passion really was
at the earliest stages of company creation. So while it was very sad to leave a company that I still
care about, you know, to this day I'm like, you know what? Facebook's going to be fine. They have an incredible set of people
kind of taking it forward, so I left. And then Ruchi, me and Akhil with the three
co-founders of Cove, and we were working on a modern collaboration software company. And, you know, our realization really was that it is
still way too difficult for knowledge workers to communicate and collaborate on all of the work that they have. It's all stuck behind,
kind of like intranets and lands and file servers. So how do we really take all of that information, and bad
communication into it, and kind of make it a first class citizen for people to be able to use in their workplaces? We've been working on it for a couple of years.
You know, we were going along quite well. We had a bunch of, strong early kind of like users. We had raised a bunch of capital
COVE was progressing quite well. And essentially then Drew and Arash were
the two co-founders of Dropbox, decided like, hey guys, do you want to join forces? Dropbox is also being used
to essentially improve collaboration. Our north stars are very similar. So why don't we join forces?
They bought our company after the acquisition. I was, the chief technology officer there. At Facebook, one of the common taglines on the wall was
do not let perfect be the enemy of good. And at Dropbox, you know, kind of a good tagline, actually.
And there were a number. But like a small like the important ones sweat the details.
Like get all of the small details right? Because if you screw up one of them,
a product will not, like feel great. And I do think that those are pretty different things. They were both cultures that really valued amazing
technology, strong product and great design. These were things that applied to both Facebook and Dropbox,
but I do think some things were different. A big one was that at Facebook, historically,
we were move fast and break things. And I think some of that was because in the early days,
Facebook was not really operating in mission critical environments. If you were trying to share a photo of a friend
or something and you know you had to repeat that action 2 or 3 times, not the end of the world. So we could adopt a lot of, I would say, practices that were
designed to fail fast but allow for some bugginess. Like that was kind of our overriding
philosophy at Dropbox, though. One of the key differences in our culture was that,
throughout our culture, it was very much like you had to be ultra reliable,
ultra low latency, ultra high throughput, ultra secure. And the analogy I give people is that if one out of every
thousand times you try to access facebook.com and it doesn't work, you're like, whatever, I'll retry it. Once out of every thousand times your hard drive
fails on you, you will think your computer is broken. It was this fundamental realization which I
think ended up really affecting large parts of both companies culture in many different ways. You know, over the years, I think what I've come to,
what I tell my startups today is that there is no one right or wrong culture, right? Like, do not try to go and take Google's Amazon's,
Facebook's or Stripe's whatever culture and put it onto your company. Find out like the culture and the values
that make sense for your mission, for your product. So I think it's both a question
of finding out what works for you. And then once you find out and you
articulate it, make sure you grow it. You know, the role of a CTO. The North Star that I had as a CTO is that I
deeply cared about making sure that we were making good technical decisions, and also that our
team was operating at like maximal, productivity. We are getting the world's best engineers
to come and join us on this mission. I want to give them the best place to work at in terms
of the amount of leverage that they have and in terms of the tooling, the code base and everything. With that North Star every six months, I would say
how to do that change, satisfying that constraint at like when the engineering team is 20 people
or when I joined, when we got acquired, it was 12 people to when I left it was 1500 2000 people. Like those are pretty different things
at a fast growing company. I mean, I'll talk about this for the CTO,
but I think this is actually important for any manager executive leader at a fast growing company. Is that the most dangerous thing is you
think you have your job figured out, right? Because the job will be different in six months. And if you are doing the same things today as you were
a year ago, you're probably doing a bunch of things wrong. And this comes back to what we talked about earlier. I think that one of my favorite taglines is that the the
only thing that remains constant in hyper growth is change. I think after leaving Dropbox, I was definitely like I
was deep in the rabbit hole of like, you know, I've been lucky enough to work at a number of different amazing
companies, you know, like Facebook, Cove, Dropbox, Flipkart. I've built helped to build a bunch
of products that I'm very proud of. I've made a bunch of money.
Yet there's a question like what is the point? Why am I doing what I'm doing?
It took me a while to figure out. I kind of realized that I like building things
I like building it with, I would say driven, highly connected, like highly motivated teams. I like operating at the frontier. You know, 200 years ago, I would have been
the first people to come out to the gold kind of the Gold Coast, like, you know, California. I like being at the frontier of things.
And for me, I love the act of creation. It's like Prometheus discovering fire.
Like I created something from nothing. That's a pretty amazing, intoxicating feeling, if you will.
Right. It was pretty clear that, like,
I was able to do those things in a really powerful and leveraged way at South Park Commons. We have tried to build South Park Commons,
is this realization that you need some time to figure out what you are going to build? And I think a lot of these accelerators are
really designed to, by definition, accelerate. Right.
And our take is that, well, you might want to go slow first. Right. Like take your time, figure out which mountain
you want to climb. -1 to 0 is when you're figuring out which mountain you want to go climb. You know, zero being the base of the mountain. And then, you know, phase one is, you know, kind of base
camp to camp one, to camp four to kind of like the summit. It's something unique that we have
come up with at South Park Commons. And I think previously to South Park Commons,
you were supposed to go figure out the mountain in your own living room and we're like, no, come and do it at SPC. We're going to provide you with the support to do that.
So what support do we provide? The first thing is that it's
important to give people a physical home. So we have a physical place
in San Francisco and in New York. You know, sometimes when you leave a company or a startup,
it can feel really disorienting because you kind of went to this place, you woke up every day. This was an important part of your life.
You went to this office, you lived your life. You built your things there. And then suddenly one day, you're no longer at this startup
or office or company, and you don't know what to do. So it's important to give people a place
that they can go to once they are there. I'd say one of the biggest things that we provide is like
a highly carefully curated community of other people who are really smart, really driven, and are also in the same phase. Right? Because think about it, it's very lonely
to figure out what you want to work on. And instead what we are saying is that don't worry, we are
the smart people who are also in that same phase, right? Like you will make better decisions,
find better mountains if you interact with those people. I would say that is maybe one of the most important things
that we do, that we give people a chance to find each other in this phase, in this -1 to 0 phase. There's another part to it, which is that we provide
what we call programing or scaffolding. And a lot of our philosophy in kind of that part is
we cannot give people a playbook to start a company. There is no course I can teach. There is no template, checklist, project,
whatever I can give them. But what I can do is I can come
up with ways of bootstrapping creativity. I can help you turn that blank piece
of paper into ten interesting ideas. I can give you ways of discussing
those ideas with other smart people. I can give you a nudge to go build, to write
that first line of code, to design that first pixel, maybe to have that first customer conversation. So we have a lot of programs that help you kind
of like get started, because it's always that first line of code that's the hardest, you know. But once you get going, I know that everybody
at SPC is technical and they can build something. And the last thing is,
say we're very generous with our time. Anybody at SPC, they can come find time with me,
with Ruchi, with our other partners. We're all, you know, I would say we have been doing
this for a while, and we don't differentiate between people who we have funded versus not. If you're at SPC, come talk to us.
We'll I'll give you feedback on the idea. Right. Like once you start climbing, you can go fast. Great. But it's more important to identify the mountain. So yeah. So you know what a grant was, saying that like, I want
to take the time to do category creation. By the way category creation,
hardest thing to do for a startup. It is really hard right. Like it is much easier to go take an
existing category, build another product. Category creation is in some ways the hardest,
hardest part of an already hard thing, which is the startup. So I do think that like,
do we encourage founders to take bigger risks? Absolutely. Like I think the most fun part of my job in some ways,
but also in sometimes the hardest, is that to convince a founder like, hey, your idea is good, you can
probably get funding, but I don't think you should do it. I actually want you to throw away
this good thing in pursuit of a great one. And this is in some ways,
another way to explain why SPC exists. I want people to take the biggest risks,
take the biggest swings, find the biggest mountain. And that's kind of been our calling from day one.

Aditya Agarwal’s journey at Facebook began in 2005, soon after meeting Mark Zuckerberg through an acquaintance.   
  
As one of Facebook’s early engineers, Agarwal was tasked with building the company’s search engine. He later successfully developed the search engine and became Facebook’s first Director of Product Engineering.   
  
After leaving Facebook in 2010, Agarwal took on leadership roles in various tech companies.   
  
He is now a partner at South Park Commons, a collective in San Francisco and New York with over 500 members, including founders and employees at Google Brain, OpenAI, and the Chan Zuckerberg Initiative.
